question: Using the customary setting of the mathematics used for quantum mechanics, is it possible to prove the existence of Gödelßs god-like entities?

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The mathematics that is actually used in the customary formulation of quantum mechanics is the mathematics of complex separable Hilbert spaces, bounded self-adjoint operators, spectral measures and the associated C*-algebraic/functional analytic framework, all formalised in ordinary classical first-order set theory. That framework furnishes a classical propositional and predicate logic with the usual Boolean algebra of projections only up to the orthocomplementation of closed subspaces, and it has no canonical internal notion of metaphysical necessity/possibility.

Gödel’s ontological argument is an argument in quantified modal logic S5. Its soundness requires a Kripke frame with a reflexive, transitive, symmetric accessibility relation and the usual modal axioms K, T, 4, 5 together with the standard Gödel axioms for a positive property and God-like essence. While S5 can be studied as abstract metalogic, there is no natural, interpretation-preserving embedding of such a frame into the Hilbert-space structure used in quantum theory. In particular the lattice L(H) of closed subspaces of a Hilbert space is orthomodular and non-distributive for dim H ≥3, so the Boolean algebra of propositions that underlies classical modal semantics is not available internally, and the Kochen–Specker contextuality phenomenon precludes a non-contextual valuation of the modal operators that Gödel’s proof manipulates.

Hence the proof cannot be carried out within the customary mathematical setting of quantum mechanics itself; one must move to an external classical modal metalanguage, i.e. to Kripke semantics formulated outside the Hilbert-space formalism, in order to state the argument at all. Inside the standard quantum-mechanical mathematics there is no way to realise the S5 necessity operator and the divine essence axioms in a consistent, interpretation-preserving way, so the existence of Gödel god-like entities is not provable in that setting.

The ontological argument is a purely logical statement about the concept
``positive property'' in classical modal logic S5.  In the form in which
Gödel wrote it down it is

* P(x) is positive iff P is ``positive'' in the intuitive sense,
* P is positive $\to$ $\Diamond\exists x\,P(x)$,
* P is positive $\to$ $[\,\neg P(x)\to \neg P(x)\,$ is positive],
* $\Box\,\forall P\,[P({\rm G})\to \Box P({\rm G})]$ etc,

from which $\exists x\,{\rm Ess}x{\rm G}$ and $\Box\exists x{\rm G}(x)$ is
derived in S5.  The derivation is a derivation in first order modal
logic.  First order modal logic is a fragment of ZF set theory.  ZF
set theory is the meta-theory in which the Hilbert space $L^{2}({\mathbb
C})$, the self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem and the whole
customary mathematics of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is
formalised.  Hence syntactically you can write Gödel’s axioms and the
derivation down in the same set theory which is the background of the
quantum formalism.

What you cannot get is a physical theorem of quantum mechanics.  The
proof is conditional on the de re metaphysical axiom that the class of
positive properties is closed under conjunction, under implication, is
absolute under $\Box$, etc. That is not a theorem of the Hilbert-space
calculus, it is an extra-logical stipulation about ``god-likeness''.
In particular if the propositions of the theory are read in the
conventional quantum-logical way, i.e. as the orthomodular lattice
${\cal L}({\cal H})$ of closed subspaces of a (complex) Hilbert space,
the lattice is non-distributive and non-Boolean.  The classical
propositional calculus and the S5 modal calculus on which Gödel’s
derivation rests is not the logic of the physical propositions of
quantum mechanics.  The existential claim $\exists x\,{\rm G}(x)$ is
therefore not a consequence of the Hilbert-space formalism and it has
no operational content in quantum theory.  In the normal physical sense
of “prove in the mathematics used for quantum mechanics’’ the
ontological conclusion is vacuous; the formal modal derivation can be
coded in the metatheory, but it gives no theorem of physics and it
fails as a quantum-logical statement about a physical system.

quantum mechanics is just ordinary classical mathematics written down in
the set theoretic language of ZFC+analysis, with classical first order
logic in the metatheory.  In that language you can write down a
first order modal language, you can write down Gödel's notion of a
positive property P, of a God-like essence G = ∀F[P(F)→E(F)], of
necessary positivity □P(F)→P(F) etc., and you can write down the S5
axioms.  Relative to those metaphysical axioms

* P(F) → □P(F),
* P(F) ∧ P(G) → P(F ∧ G),
* ∃F P(F), 
* etc.,

the usual Gödel ontological theorem

□∃x G(x) → ∃x □G(x) ,  G(x) → ∀F[P(F)→F(x)] , etc.,

is a perfectly correct theorem of propositional modal logic S5, and S5
is interpretable in ordinary set theory and hence in the foundations
that underwrite the Hilbert space formalism.

What the physics does not give you is the axioms.  The positivity
axioms, the necessity of positivity, the identification of existence
with a positive property and the S5 scheme for □ are not theorems of
functional analysis, of operator algebras on a complex Hilbert space, or
of the Born rule.  They are extra-logical, essentially metaphysical,
premises about essence and necessity.  In the customary physical use of
the mathematics the meta-theory stays classical and the content of the
theory is empirically interpreted.  Hence the Hilbert space formalism
can express the Gödel argument, but it does not prove it.  No
mathematical theorem of the ordinary mathematical physics of quantum
mechanics, and no physical prediction of quantum mechanics, entails the
existence of a Gödel God-like being without importing the
contested modal-ontological premises that Gödel himself added by hand.
In the interesting physical/metamathematical sense the existence is
therefore not proved by, and is not a consequence of, the customary
mathematics of quantum mechanics.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is whether Gödel's ontological argument for a god-like essence G = ∀F[P(F)→E(F)] with a positive property P and S5 necessity □ can be proved from, or within, the customary mathematics of quantum mechanics.

All three colleagues agree the formalism of non-relativistic quantum mechanics — separable complex Hilbert spaces, bounded self-adjoint operators, spectral measures, C*-algebras — is formalised in ordinary classical set theory ZFC + analysis with classical first-order logic as meta-theory. Hence syntactically the quantified modal S5 language of Gödel, the positivity axioms
P(F)→□P(F), P(F)∧P(G)→P(F∧G), ∃F P(F), etc., and the standard Gödel derivation □∃x G(x)→∃x □G(x), G(x)→∀F[P(F)→F(x)] can be written down in the same meta-theory that underwrites the Hilbert space apparatus. In that trivial encoding sense the derivation is a theorem of S5 and is interpretable in set theory.

The substantive disagreement is about physical/internal provability. Colleague 1: the Hilbert space apparatus can express the argument but does not supply the modal-ontological premises; positivity, necessity of positivity, identification of existence with a positive property and the S5 scheme for □ are extra-logical metaphysical premises, not theorems of functional analysis or the Born rule.

Colleague 2 stresses the lack of an internal modal semantics: the mathematics used has no canonical internal notion of metaphysical necessity/possibility. The lattice L(H) of closed subspaces is orthomodular and non-distributive for dim H ≥3, so the Boolean algebra of propositions required for classical modal semantics is not available internally, and Kochen-Specker contextuality precludes a non-contextual valuation of the modal operators Gödel manipulates. Therefore the proof cannot be carried out interpretation-preserving inside the Hilbert-space structure; an external classical modal metalanguage is needed.

Colleague 3 concurs: the derivation is a first-order modal derivation, a fragment of ZF, so it can be coded in the meta-theory, but it is conditional on de re metaphysical closure axioms for positive properties that are not theorems of the Hilbert-space calculus. Read physically, propositions are the orthomodular lattice L(H), not a Boolean algebra, so the classical propositional and S5 modal calculus on which Gödel rests is not the logic of physical propositions of QM. Hence ∃x G(x) is not a consequence of the Hilbert-space formalism and has no operational content in quantum theory.

Current synthesis: In the normal physical/mathematical sense of “prove using the mathematics of quantum mechanics”, no. The customary mathematics is classical set theory, so the Gödel argument can be formally encoded in the meta-theory, but the modal axioms and positivity premises are not derived from, nor are they part of, the Hilbert space/C*-algebraic framework, and there is no natural internal S5 necessity operator in quantum logic. Existence of Gödel god-like entities is therefore not proved by, and is not a consequence of, the customary physics mathematics without importing contested extra-logical modal-ontological premises.

Unresolved nuance: whether mere syntactic encodability in the same set-theoretic meta-theory counts as “possible to prove using the customary setting”. The consensus leans to no in any physically meaningful internal sense, yes only trivially in the meta-theoretic coding sense.
